title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — October 14, 2026 (Two Portuguese Cities Meet Their First Real Evidence)
headline: Lisbon and Porto's first real checks measure 35.0 and 32.5; both published scores stay at 60.9.
summary:
Nothing in this briefing has been applied. Every score named as published is the live score. Every other number is a proposal or a measurement.

Lisbon and Porto had never been checked against evidence. Each carried a published 60.9 out of 100, a starting value shared with other unmeasured cities. A first full assessment measures Lisbon at 35.0 and Porto at 32.5. Both readings are low confidence, and both would cross from the Established band to the Developing band. This is a first measurement, not a measured decline in conduct.

Lisbon's reading rests most on the Glória funicular crash of 3 September 2025, which killed 16 people. Portugal's state accident investigator (GPIAAF) found that the city-owned bus company Carris ran it on a cable not certified for passengers. Porto's reading follows the 12 October 2026 removal of a housing-protest camp, which the council called an illegal occupation.

Where evidence is missing, these assessments score the gap at 2 out of 5. Scoring the gaps at the middle value of 3 would give Lisbon 41.9 and Porto 40.6, both still below Established.

Cornell University measures 41.9 again, matching the proposal filed on 1 October. Its published score is 54.7. Eight other published readings held: India, Delhi, Texas, Tennessee, Sudan, the United States, Russia and the UAE.

Release watch: 0 sources registered — detection did not run.

topSignals.title: Lisbon's 60.9 Was a Starting Value; Its First Real Check Measures 35.0
topSignals.whyItMatters: Lisbon's published 60.9 came from a template number, not research. A first evidence-based reading is 35.0. The city's homeless count earned credit. A fatal funicular crash and slow compensation did not.
topSignals.description:
Lisbon is ranked 33rd among global cities with a published score of 60.9 out of 100, in the Established band (60 to 80). That number was never checked against evidence. A first full assessment measures 35.0, in the Developing band (20 to 40), with low confidence. The published score is unchanged, and the proposed change has not been applied.

This is a first measurement, not a measured decline in conduct. The assessment scores the city government and its companies. National housing and rent law, the main target of the 10 October 2026 housing protests, is excluded.

The heaviest evidence is the Glória funicular crash of 3 September 2025, which killed 16 people. The city-owned company Carris ran the funicular on a cable not certified for passengers, and maintenance logged as done was not always carried out, according to the preliminary finding of Portugal's state accident investigator, the GPIAAF. Compensation has been slow. By 27 August 2026 the insurer had made four payments to families of people killed, according to ECO.

The credit side is homelessness. Lisbon counts its homeless population each year and runs a 2024-2030 homeless plan. Its count fell from 3,378 to 3,122, according to RTP.

Eleven of the 40 sub-measures have no evidence and are scored at 2 out of 5. At the middle value of 3, the reading would be 41.9, in the Functional band (40 to 60), still below Established.

evidence.quote: não está certificado para instalações de transporte de pessoas
evidence.claim: The cable used by the city-owned company Carris on the Glória funicular was not certified for passenger transport, according to the preliminary finding of Portugal's state accident investigator (GPIAAF).

evidence.quote: tarefas de manutenção registadas como cumpridas nem sempre correspondem às tarefas efetivamente realizadas
evidence.claim: Maintenance that Carris logged as done was not always carried out (GPIAAF).

evidence.claim: Lisbon's deputy mayor called still-open Glória compensation cases normal about ten months after the accident.
Carris's insurer had assumed EUR 2.3 million of costs, including four compensation payments to families of people killed, by 27 August 2026.

topSignals.title: Porto's 60.9 Was a Starting Value; Its First Real Check Measures 32.5
topSignals.whyItMatters: Porto's published 60.9 was never measured. A first reading is 32.5, at low confidence. The city cut street homelessness, but it cleared a housing-protest camp on 12 October 2026, and the adverse sources are press and council statements.
topSignals.description:
Porto is ranked 34th among global cities with a published score of 60.9 out of 100, in the Established band. That number was never checked against evidence. A first full assessment measures 32.5, in the Developing band, with low confidence. The published score is unchanged, and the proposed change has not been applied.

On 12 October 2026 the municipal police, the national police (PSP) and the city company Porto Ambiente removed a housing-protest camp in Praça D. João I. The council said it was not allowing illegal occupation and degradation of public space, according to a council statement relayed by Lusa. A camp participant told RTP that no justification was given. The assessment charges the city's share of the action, not the national police's.

The credit side is homelessness. Council data show 526 homeless people in 2025, down from 730 in 2021, and the city runs a subsidised-rent programme. Local charities said Housing First, which gives homeless people a permanent home first, served only six people in 2025, according to RTP and Lusa.

The adverse items are a council statement and press testimony. No court, government or international-body source was found, so the band crossing is held at low confidence. Thirteen of the 40 sub-measures have no evidence and are scored at 2 out of 5. At the middle value of 3, the reading would be 40.6, in the Functional band, 0.6 points above the line with Developing.

evidence.source: Câmara Municipal do Porto statement (Lusa via DNotícias)

evidence.claim: A camp participant said no justification was given for the removal.

evidence.claim: Credited: council data show 526 homeless people in 2025, down from 730 in 2021.

topSignals.title: Cornell's Pending 41.9 Is Matched by a New Reading After the State Names a Special Prosecutor
topSignals.whyItMatters: New York's attorney general is now special prosecutor in an alleged 2024 assault case. A fresh reading of Cornell again measures 41.9. Cornell's published score is still 54.7.
topSignals.description:
Cornell University is ranked 12th among 100 universities at a published 54.7 out of 100, in the Functional band. A proposal filed on 1 October 2026 puts it at 41.9, also Functional. Today's separate reading measures 41.9 again, so no new proposal was filed. The published score is unchanged, and nothing has been applied.

On 1 October 2026 Governor Kathy Hochul named Attorney General Letitia James special prosecutor in the alleged 2024 sexual assault of a Cornell student, according to Reuters via The Star. Hochul said new information raised questions about the Cornell Police investigation and the county prosecutor's decision not to charge anyone. Those questions are the governor's, not findings. The lawsuit's allegations are not scored as fact.

The assessment scores what Cornell itself did. It is credited for expelling students and closing a fraternity chapter. It has not acknowledged any failure in its handling, and its 21 September 2026 statement routes the response to the legal process.

evidence.claim: On 1 October 2026 New York Governor Kathy Hochul named Attorney General Letitia James special prosecutor in the alleged 2024 sexual assault of a Cornell student, citing new information that raised questions about the Cornell Police investigation.

evidence.quote: The New York state attorney general announced a review of the university's initial response to the allegations.
evidence.claim: The NY Attorney General announced a review of Cornell's initial response.

evidence.quote: Cornell University is aware of a lawsuit concerning the deeply disturbing allegations of sexual assault involving members of the student community that occurred in 2024.
evidence.claim: Cornell's institutional response to the lawsuit.

topSignals.title: India Called a UN Concern About Mass Detentions 'Unwarranted Interference'
topSignals.whyItMatters: On 10 October 2026 the UN human rights office raised concern over mass detentions around Delhi protests. India's reply lowers one measure, Validation, but India's total stays at 15.6 out of 100.
topSignals.description:
India's published score is 15.6 out of 100, in the Critical band (0 to 20). The new reading is also 15.6. The published score is confirmed and unchanged.

On 10 October 2026 the UN Human Rights Office said it was concerned by mass detentions of protesters, lawyers and journalists around Delhi protests, according to The News Minute. India's Permanent Mission in Geneva rejected the concern as misplaced and unwarranted interference, according to DT Next. Detainees were released the same evening. No independent count of the detentions exists, and the figure of about 1,000 comes from police sources, so it is not used.

One sub-measure, Validation (does the government take criticism seriously?), drops from 2 to 1 out of 5 because the concern was rebuffed, not examined. That lowers Empathy by 0.2 and leaves the total at 15.6.

evidence.claim: On 10 October 2026 the UN Human Rights Office said it was concerned by mass detentions of protesters, lawyers and journalists around Delhi protests and asked India to release anyone arbitrarily detained.
India's Permanent Mission in Geneva rejected the concern as misplaced and unwarranted interference.

topSignals.title: Texas Carried Out an Execution a Week After the Same Drug Failed in Tennessee
topSignals.whyItMatters: Texas executed Jamaal Howard on 7 October 2026 and did not answer a request to pause. The practice is already in Texas's 38.8 out of 100, so the score is confirmed.
topSignals.description:
Texas's published score is 38.8 out of 100, in the Developing band. The new reading is also 38.8. The published score is confirmed and unchanged.

Texas executed Jamaal Howard on 7 October 2026, its seventh execution of the year, a week after the same lethal-injection drug failed in Tennessee, according to the Texas Tribune. Lawyers said the State would not show them the drug's testing history. That is a caution on Transparency, which stays at 4 out of 5 on the strength of State Auditor reports.

Texas sits 1.2 points below the Functional line at 40.

evidence.claim: Texas executed Jamaal Howard on 7 October 2026, a week after the same lethal-injection drug failed in Tennessee; lawyers said the State would not show them the drug's testing history.

topSignals.title: Tennessee's Prisons Chief Is Resigning; the Halt and Outside Review Were Already Credited
topSignals.whyItMatters: Tennessee has had two failed executions in 2026. Its prisons chief is leaving but says protocol was followed. A named outside reviewer now leads the inquiry. The reading is 29.4; the published score is 30.0.
topSignals.description:
Tennessee's published score is 30.0 out of 100, in the Developing band. The new reading is 29.4, within the 5-point threshold. The published score is confirmed and unchanged.

The state's prisons chief, Commissioner Strada, is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike while maintaining that protocol was followed, according to AP via WBTV on 3 October 2026. Former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton was named to lead the third-party review. Governor Bill Lee had already halted executions on 1 October, according to WPLN, and that was credited. The terms of the Stanton review are not yet public.

evidence.claim: Tennessee's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike while maintaining the protocol was followed; former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton was named to lead the review.
After the failed execution of Christa Pike, Governor Bill Lee halted executions and ordered a third-party review.

emergingRisks.risk: Published scores that were never measured may sit well above what a first reading of the evidence supports.
emergingRisks.detail: Across four proposal cycles, 14 first baselines have produced 13 lower readings and one higher one. Lisbon (35.0 measured) and Porto (32.5 measured) join Madrid and Valencia as Iberian cities that read far below their starting values. Gap values also differ between runs: at 3 instead of 2, Lisbon would read 41.9 and Porto 40.6.

emergingRisks.risk: Portugal's housing protests may bring more camp removals, and a court or ombudsman record would raise the evidence quality behind Porto's reading.
emergingRisks.detail: Thousands marched in Lisbon and about 1,500 in Porto on 10 October 2026, according to Euronews. Porto removed the resulting camp on 12 October. National housing law, the protests' main target, is outside the city scores.

emergingRisks.risk: New York's special-prosecutor inquiry into the Cornell case may produce findings about the university police investigation.
emergingRisks.detail: Governor Hochul named the attorney general special prosecutor on 1 October 2026. Until there are findings, the questions about the police investigation remain the governor's, and the allegations remain allegations.

emergingRisks.risk: Two US states carried out or attempted executions with the same drug within a week, and Tennessee's halt may not outlast the next change of governor.
emergingRisks.detail: Texas executed Jamaal Howard on 7 October 2026 after the drug failed in Tennessee on 30 September. Tennessee's outside review has no published terms of reference.

emergingRisks.risk: Attacks on food-aid convoys in Sudan deepen the famine risk in a country already at the lowest score.
emergingRisks.detail: A World Food Programme-contracted driver was killed on 3 October 2026 in South Kordofan. No party was named. Sudan cannot fall further, so the effect shows in aid access, not the score.

sectorAlerts.sector: Global Cities — Two Portuguese Cities Meet Their First Real Evidence
sectorAlerts.headline: Lisbon and Porto both read about 26 to 28 points below never-measured starting values of 60.9.
observations: Lisbon: published 60.9, measured 35.0, at low confidence. The Glória funicular crash and slow compensation weigh most; the homeless count is credited.
Porto: published 60.9, measured 32.5, at low confidence. The 12 October 2026 camp removal weighs against the city; the fall in homelessness from 730 to 526 is credited.
Madrid (65.6 published, 48.1 proposed) and Valencia (60.9 published, 41.9 proposed) were the earlier Iberian first readings. All four read far below their starting values.
Delhi stays at a published 32.8. A reading of 28.1 for the third time is 4.7 points lower, under the 5-point threshold, because Delhi Police answers to the national Home Ministry.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries — Detentions, Convoy Attacks and a Floor That Cannot Fall Further
sectorAlerts.headline: India, the United States and the UAE each held within the 5-point threshold; Sudan and Russia stay at 0.
observations: India stays at 15.6 after rejecting a UN concern over mass detentions around Delhi protests.
The United States reads 16.3 against a published 17.5. The 2 October 2026 detention of an asylum seeker repeats a practice scored on 17 September.
The UAE reads 15.0 against a published 18.4 in its first full 40-measure scoring. Human Rights Watch's 7 October 2026 EU letter adds advocacy, not new conduct.
Sudan and Russia stay at 0 of 100: a food-aid driver was killed on 3 October, and a state-owned plant explosion on 1 October has an unsettled toll.

methodologyNotes.name: A First Measurement Is Not a Decline
methodologyNotes.description: Lisbon and Porto had never been checked against evidence. Their published 60.9 was a starting value shared by many unmeasured cities. A first reading describes what the benchmark did not yet know, not what the city did differently this week.

methodologyNotes.name: Evidence Gaps Are Scored Low, So the Gap Value Matters
methodologyNotes.description: Lisbon has 11 sub-measures with no evidence and Porto has 13. Both assessments score a gap at 2 out of 5. At the middle value of 3, Lisbon would read 41.9 and Porto 40.6. Earlier first readings used different gap values, so the benchmark is settling on one convention.

methodologyNotes.name: Source Quality Gates Band Crossings
methodologyNotes.description: A proposal that crosses a band line needs at least one strong source, such as a court, government or international body. Lisbon clears that bar through Portugal's state accident investigator. Porto's adverse items are a council statement and press testimony, so its crossing is held at low confidence.

methodologyNotes.name: Allegations Are Not Scored as Facts
methodologyNotes.description: The Cornell lawsuit's allegations, and the governor's questions about the police investigation, are not findings. The benchmark scores what Cornell itself did and said.

methodologyNotes.name: We Score Who Caused the Harm
methodologyNotes.description: Delhi Police reports to India's national government, so the 10 October 2026 detentions are scored under India, not Delhi. The national police's part in Porto's camp removal, and national housing law in Lisbon, are not charged to the cities.

methodologyNotes.name: The Same Conduct Is Not Scored Twice
methodologyNotes.description: Texas's execution practice and the United States' detention of asylum seekers were scored in earlier cycles. A new event of the same kind confirms the earlier reading but does not move it again.

dailyOpeningQuestion.text: Lisbon's band crossing rests on Portugal's state accident investigator; does Porto's 12 October 2026 camp removal have a court, government or ombudsman record that meets the same source-quality rule for a band crossing?
dailyOpeningQuestion.tensionFraming: Two Portuguese cities share a 60.9 starting value and both read far lower, but only one has the source quality the crossing rule requires.
